# **Advanced Computational, Optimization, and Learning Frameworks for the Furuta Rotary Inverted Pendulum**

## **Modern Physics Simulation Engines and Multibody Dynamics Environments**

The physical dynamics of the Furuta rotary inverted pendulum are characterized by kinematic coupling, an underactuated configuration space defined on the non-Euclidean manifold $S^1 \times S^1$, and open-loop instability about its upright equilibrium1. Originating from the 1991 benchmark formulation by Katsuhisa Furuta at the Tokyo Institute of Technology, the mechanism isolates the fundamental balance challenges found in rocketry thrust-vector control, bipedal humanoid walking, crane payload sway mitigation, and personal balancing transporters1. Accurate numerical simulation, offline trajectory synthesis, and data-driven policy learning require simulation engines capable of resolving stiff differential-algebraic equations without numerical dissipation or artificial coordinate drift1. While academic mechatronics curricula frequently standardize on analytical ordinary differential equation solvers or MATLAB Simscape Multibody blocks1, contemporary robotics engineering utilizes specialized simulation platforms that balance parallel throughput, analytical mechanics, and physical contact modeling9.  
The landscape of modern simulation engines splits into three distinct architectural paradigms. MuJoCo focuses on continuous multi-body contact dynamics and minimal coordinate representations, making it effective for zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and continuous control benchmarking9. The Drake simulation platform emphasizes analytical mechanics, symbolic computation, and sum-of-squares optimization, providing certified stability regions and mathematically verified invariant sets13. NVIDIA Isaac Lab leverages massively parallel GPU simulation pipelines via PhysX, running thousands of environment instances concurrently to train complex reinforcement learning policies within short timeframes11.

### **MuJoCo: Fast Continuous Dynamics and Sim-to-Real Fidelity**

MuJoCo (Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact) has established itself as a primary simulation environment for continuous control benchmarks and physical reinforcement learning9. Formulated using generalized minimal coordinates, the engine eliminates the numerical drift and artificial joint separation common in maximal-coordinate game engines5. The Furuta pendulum is modeled via an XML-based MJCF description featuring a fixed world anchor, an actuated revolute joint defining the horizontal arm ($\theta_0$), and an unactuated revolute joint defining the vertical pendulum link ($\theta_1$)1.  
MuJoCo resolves non-conservative joint behaviors through explicit parameters governing viscous damping, dry Coulomb friction, and actuator rotor armature inertia5. This inclusion of reflected rotor inertia is essential, as the high angular accelerations of the base servomotor introduce significant inertial resistance into the horizontal joint dynamics5. Using semi-implicit Euler or fourth-order Runge-Kutta numerical integration at sub-millisecond timesteps, MuJoCo executes at rates exceeding 50,000 steps per second on single CPU threads9. Native Python bindings allow researchers to wrap the underlying C dynamic engine within standardized Gymnasium environments, exposing direct armature voltage or torque interfaces that match physical motor drivers9.

### **Drake: Analytical Mechanics, Sums-of-Squares Optimization, and Stability Certificates**

Developed by the MIT Robot Locomotion Group, Drake approaches underactuated mechanics through analytical dynamics and convex optimization rather than sampling heuristics13. Drake instantiates the rotary pendulum as a MultibodyPlant associated with a SceneGraph geometry engine, parsing either Universal Robot Description Format (URDF) or programmatic system definitions13.  
The primary advantage of Drake lies in its mathematical certification tools13. Classical Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) designs operate under the assumption of localized linearization, which leaves the true operational boundaries of the balancing controller unquantified1. Drake addresses this limitation by automating the computation of certified Regions of Attraction (ROA) via Sums-of-Squares (SOS) polynomial optimization14. By formulating polynomial approximations of the closed-loop pendulum dynamics, Drake’s MathematicalProgram interface solves semidefinite programs (SDPs) to certify invariant sublevel sets $V(x) \le \rho$ around the upright vertical equilibrium14. Trajectories originating within this certified boundary are mathematically guaranteed to converge to the inverted configuration15.  
Additionally, Drake provides native trajectory transcription routines, such as DirectCollocation, which convert nonlinear differential equations into constrained optimization problems15. These routines solve for minimum-effort swing-up trajectories that respect motor torque and horizontal arm excursion limits, providing verified reference paths for tracking controllers15.

### **NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab: Parallelized GPU Vectorization**

When training model-free reinforcement learning policies, sample complexity poses a significant computational bottleneck9. NVIDIA Isaac Lab addresses this by shifting physics simulation directly to GPU Tensor and CUDA cores, bypassing the latency of CPU-to-GPU data transfers11. Using vectorized PhysX pipelines, Isaac Lab simulates thousands of independent Furuta pendulum instances in parallel within a single graphics workstation11.  
Isaac Lab features two distinct design models: a Manager-Based workflow that decouples rewards, observations, and termination conditions into modular classes, and a Direct workflow that executes an optimized, single-class structure following the Gymnasium API11. For low-degree-of-freedom mechanisms like the Furuta pendulum, the Direct workflow achieves aggregate simulation throughput exceeding 200,000 steps per second11. This throughput allows on-policy algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to converge in minutes rather than hours, while simultaneously executing wide-range domain randomization sweeps across physical link parameters and joint friction coefficients11.

## **Trajectory Optimization, Differential Dynamic Programming, and Embedded NMPC**

While heuristic energy-shaping methods (such as the Åström-Furuta strategy) reliably generate swing-up maneuvers1, they cannot enforce state constraints—such as keeping the horizontal arm within a safe workspace—or minimize control energy3. Numerical trajectory optimization approaches formulate both the swing-up and stabilization of the Furuta pendulum as an optimal control problem (OCP) solved over finite time horizons31.

### **Rigid-Body Dynamics and Differential Dynamic Programming: Pinocchio and Crocoddyl**

The integration of Pinocchio and Crocoddyl provides an efficient framework for trajectory optimization on multi-body systems9. Pinocchio computes rigid-body spatial vector operations—including the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm (RNEA) for inverse dynamics and the Articulated Body Algorithm (ABA) for forward dynamics—along with their analytical derivatives $\frac{\partial \text{ABA}}{\partial q}$ and $\frac{\partial \text{ABA}}{\partial v}$ using analytical C++ spatial algebra5.  
Crocoddyl utilizes these analytical derivatives to solve discrete-time optimal control problems via Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) and box-constrained iterative Linear Quadratic Regulation (iLQR)9:

$$\min_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \ell_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) + \ell_N(\mathbf{x}_N) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k), \quad \mathbf{u}_{\min} \le \mathbf{u}_k \le \mathbf{u}_{\max}$$

During the backward pass, Crocoddyl evaluates dynamic quadratizations of the Hamiltonian around nominal state-action trajectories31. This computation yields an updated feedforward control sequence $\mathbf{u}_k^*$ alongside a sequence of linear feedback gain matrices $\mathbf{K}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 4}$31:

$$\mathbf{u}_k(\mathbf{x}_k) = \mathbf{u}_k^* - \mathbf{K}_k (\mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_k^*)$$

This formulation generates a time-varying linear feedback policy (LTV-LQR) directly along the swing-up trajectory, providing stabilization against disturbances before the system enters the upright equilibrium basin31. Armand du Parc Locmaria and Pierre Fabre implemented this architecture in the open-source Armandpl/furuta platform, demonstrating that Crocoddyl generates minimum-time, torque-bounded swing-up sequences without requiring manual switching heuristic tuning6.

### **Direct Multiple Shooting and Algorithmic Differentiation: CasADi and IPOPT**

CasADi provides a symbolic framework for nonlinear optimization and automatic differentiation via forward and reverse mode computation graphs32. In direct multiple shooting formulations, the continuous time interval $[0, T]$ is partitioned into $N$ shooting intervals33. The system state vector $\mathbf{x}_k = [\theta_0, \theta_1, \dot{\theta}_0, \dot{\theta}_1]^T$ and control input $u_k = V_m$ serve as decision variables within a sparse Non-Linear Program (NLP)1:

$$\min_{\mathbf{x}_0, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N, u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left( \Vert{}\mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_{\text{goal}}\Vert{}_{\mathbf{Q}}^2 + \Vert{}u_k\Vert{}_{\mathbf{R}}^2 \right) + \Vert{}\mathbf{x}_N - \mathbf{x}_{\text{goal}}\Vert{}_{\mathbf{P}}^2$$

$$\text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{x}_{k+1} - \mathbf{\Phi}(\mathbf{x}_k, u_k) = 0, \quad k=0, \dots, N-1$$

$$\mathbf{x}_{\min} \le \mathbf{x}_k \le \mathbf{x}_{\max}, \quad u_{\min} \le u_k \le u_{\max}$$

The dynamic matching condition $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} - \mathbf{\Phi}(\mathbf{x}_k, u_k) = 0$ is enforced as an equality constraint, where $\mathbf{\Phi}$ represents a numerical integrator (e.g., Runge-Kutta 4) evaluated across the shooting node33. Solvers like IPOPT (Interior Point Optimizer) solve the resulting sparse Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) systems using exact Hessians, computing dynamically feasible swing-up trajectories that keep horizontal arm excursion within safe physical bounds ($\vert{}\theta_0\vert{} \le \theta_{0,\max}$)1.

### **Millisecond Nonlinear Model Predictive Control: acados**

For real-time embedded execution, solving full NLPs using IPOPT introduces unacceptable latency ($50\text{ ms} - 500\text{ ms}$), exceeding the mechanical stabilization window of inverted pendulums33. The acados framework addresses this by implementing Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) and Real-Time Iteration (RTI) schemes in optimized C, utilizing the High-Performance Interior Point Method (HPIPM) solver and BLASFEO linear algebra kernels32.  
Homburger, Frey, Diehl, and Reuter demonstrated real-time millisecond NMPC running onboard a physical Furuta pendulum platform37. By executing a single SQP iteration per sampling interval (RTI scheme) with a prediction horizon of $T = 2.0\text{ s}$ across $N = 50$ stages, acados achieves feedback computation times between $1.0\text{ ms}$ and $3.5\text{ ms}$33. This speed allows a single NMPC formulation to execute the continuous swing-up maneuver, handle state and torque inequality bounds, and transition smoothly into upright stabilization without requiring an external finite state machine or supervisory switching guards33.  
To accelerate convergence in fast mechanical systems, acados integrates Anderson Acceleration (AA) within its SQP solver36. Applied to the projected regularized exact Hessian formulation for the Furuta pendulum, Anderson Acceleration reduces the SQP iterations required to reach tight tolerances by more than 50% (from over 60 iterations down to under 30), adding negligible computational overhead (approximately $1.6\ \mu\text{s}$ per iteration)36.

## **Reinforcement Learning Libraries, Policy Architectures, and Reward Formulations**

Reinforcement learning formulates underactuated balance as a continuous Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined across states $\mathcal{S}$, actions $\mathcal{A}$, transition dynamics $\mathcal{P}$, and rewards $\mathcal{R}$43. Unlike localized linear feedback controllers that rely on small-angle assumptions1, model-free deep actor-critic architectures learn global policies that handle both swing-up and balance within a single neural network12.  
Software framework selection determines the trade-off between deployment modularity and algorithm transparency. Stable-Baselines3 (SB3) provides modular, production-tested implementations of continuous actor-critic algorithms like Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), supplemented with standardized wrappers for state normalization, frame history, and Generalized State-Dependent Exploration (gSDE)9. In contrast, CleanRL provides self-contained, single-file implementations that remove framework abstractions, exposing gradient updates directly and simplifying custom loss alterations for robotics applications47.

### **Continuous Action Algorithms: SAC vs. PPO**

While deep reinforcement learning algorithms can balance underactuated systems in simulation, their performance characteristics diverge on physical platforms:

* *Soft Actor-Critic (SAC):* As an off-policy algorithm founded on maximum entropy RL, SAC optimizes both expected cumulative return and policy entropy $\mathcal{H}(\pi(\cdot\vert{}s))$12. The entropy regularization term prevents premature convergence to local limit cycles, encouraging thorough exploration during the swing-up phase12. SAC exhibits higher sample efficiency than on-policy alternatives, requiring fewer environment steps to learn stable balancing behaviors12. In empirical benchmarks on rotary pendulum setups, SAC generates responsive control signals that recover effectively from large angular deflections12.  
* *Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO):* As an on-policy policy gradient algorithm, PPO constrains policy updates using a clipped surrogate objective10. While PPO is more sample-intensive—often requiring GPU-accelerated parallel simulation environments like Isaac Lab to train quickly—it produces smoother control signals that are less prone to high-frequency motor chattering11. Kevin Wood demonstrated that PPO policies trained in MuJoCo can be transferred to custom 3D-printed rotary inverted pendulum hardware1.

### **Observation Space Manifolds and Trigonometric Embeddings**

Passing raw joint angles $\theta \in [-\pi, \pi]$ directly to neural policy networks introduces artificial discontinuities at the $\pm \pi$ wrap-around boundary, disrupting gradient descent during swing-up3. To maintain topological continuity across the state space, rotary angles are projected into two-dimensional Euclidean embeddings3:

$$\mathbf{s}_t = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_0 & \sin\theta_0 & \cos\theta_1 & \sin\theta_1 & \dot{\theta}_0 & \dot{\theta}_1 \end{bmatrix}^T \in \mathbb{R}^6$$

where $\theta_0$ is the base arm angle and $\theta_1$ is the pendulum link deflection1. By projecting the angles into continuous sine and cosine components, the state manifold $S^1 \times S^1$ maps onto a continuous representation without numerical boundaries3. For multi-stage tasks or multi-link systems (such as rotary double inverted pendulums), the state vector can be augmented with a discrete target contextual variable $EP \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ that conditions the network on target equilibrium configurations20.

### **Reward Engineering and Action Regularization**

The structure of the scalar reward function directly influences both policy convergence and the physical longevity of the hardware9. Discontinuous step rewards produce sparse gradient feedback and encourage high-frequency bang-bang actuator commands45. Polynomial rewards can exhibit steep gradients near the vertical apex, leading to destabilizing policy updates45.  
Empirical studies indicate that continuous trigonometric cosine rewards provide smooth, well-conditioned gradients across the entire swing trajectory18:

$$R_t = c_1 \cos\theta_1 - c_2 \theta_0^2 - c_3 \dot{\theta}_1^2 - c_4 \dot{\theta}_0^2 - c_5 u_t^2 - c_6 (u_t - u_{t-1})^2$$

The action continuity regularization penalty $-c_6 (u_t - u_{t-1})^2$ penalizes rapid changes in commanded voltage9. Without this term, policies tend to command alternating maximum voltage commands, which can cause excessive actuator heating and gear wear9. Adding the action continuity cost smooths the commanded trajectories, producing motor voltage profiles comparable to classical LQR controllers9.  
Managing reinforcement learning lifecycles relies on MLOps infrastructure like Weights & Biases (W\&B)9. Integrating W\&B into pipelines such as Armandpl/furuta enables tracking decomposed reward metrics, tuning learning rates and entropy coefficients via automated Bayesian sweeps, and checkpointing network models alongside environment metadata to ensure reproducible policy deployment6.

## **Sim-to-Real Transfer Methodologies and System Identification**

Deploying policies trained in simulation directly onto physical hardware exposes discrepancies known as the reality gap1. These differences stem from unmodeled friction, bearing stiction, motor saturation, voltage drops, and communication latency52. Bridging this gap requires combining empirical system identification with simulation-side domain randomization and transport delay modeling52.  
System identification protocols extract the physical parameters needed to ground the simulation model1. Decoupled decay tests isolate link dynamics: clamping the base arm while logging the pendulum's unforced oscillations allows logarithmic decrement analysis to extract viscous damping ($b_1$) and dry friction1. Motor electromechanical constants are characterized by measuring terminal resistance ($R_m$) under locked-rotor conditions and recording the no-load saturation slope to identify back-EMF and torque constants ($k_m, k_t$)5. For higher accuracy, multi-frequency sinusoidal voltage sweeps drive the combined mechanism, using Levenberg-Marquardt nonlinear least-squares optimization to fit model parameters against physical response data18.  
To handle remaining model mismatch, domain randomization perturbs simulation parameters at the start of each training episode12. Link masses, centers of gravity, damping coefficients, and motor constants are sampled from uniform distributions centered around their nominal values. Adding Gaussian noise ($\sigma_\theta \approx 0.005\text{ rad}$, $\sigma_{\dot{\theta}} \approx 0.05\text{ rad/s}$) to state observations accounts for encoder quantization and finite-difference differentiation noise10.  
Transport delay introduces another significant operational challenge on physical hardware12. Microcontroller execution and serial communication over UART or USB inject control loop latencies between $10\text{ ms}$ and $30\text{ ms}$12. Policies trained in zero-latency simulations assume instantaneous torque delivery and can become unstable when subjected to real-world lag12. Incorporating a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue into the simulation step function buffers commanded actions by $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, training the network to anticipate system momentum and execute stable balancing maneuvers on hardware12.

## **Real-Time Telemetry, Hardware-in-the-Loop Logging, and Telemetry Visualizers**

While MATLAB App Designer provides an established dashboard for academic prototypes1, open-source robotics telemetry tools offer higher streaming rates and lower computational overhead during hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing57.  
PlotJuggler provides high-throughput time-series visualization for low-latency debugging57. Connecting directly to serial UART, UDP sockets, or ROS 2 topics, PlotJuggler processes incoming telemetry at update rates exceeding $1\text{ kHz}$57. Built-in Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) tools assist in tuning encoder velocity filter cutoff frequencies by revealing mechanical vibration and quantization noise spikes directly1. Integrated Lua scripting enables online calculation of energy metrics and cumulative error integrals (IAE, ISE, ITAE) during live operation1.  
Foxglove Studio offers a modular visualization platform centered around the open-source MCAP binary container format57. MCAP structures telemetry into indexed, compressed chunks (using lz4 or zstd), preventing file corruption during abrupt shutdowns and enabling random seeking across datasets59. Foxglove Studio synchronizes 2D time-series strip charts with an interactive 3D panel rendering the pendulum's URDF model in real time from incoming joint angles57. Recorded experimental runs can be scrubbed and replayed to directly compare hardware trajectories against simulation baselines1.  
The Rerun SDK provides multimodal data logging across synchronized timelines57. Written in Rust with bindings for Python, C++, and Rust, Rerun allows firmware or host drivers to log numeric state trajectories alongside spatial coordinate transforms57. The client can map observations across multiple temporal axes—such as simulation time, wall-clock time, and control step sequence—preserving alignment despite communication latency and facilitating policy evaluation57.

## **Embedded Execution, Micro-ROS, and TinyML Deployment Frameworks**

Deploying control algorithms onto embedded microcontrollers requires meeting real-time execution constraints1. While baseline academic projects often implement continuous state-space controllers directly within MATLAB Simulink and compile via Embedded Coder1, alternative embedded stacks offer greater autonomy, reduced memory footprints, and broader framework compatibility69.  
Micro-ROS extends the Robot Operating System (ROS 2\) directly onto resource-constrained 32-bit microcontrollers, including the STMicroelectronics STM32 (ARM Cortex-M4/M7), Espressif ESP32, and PJRC Teensy 4.11. Running atop embedded RTOSs (such as FreeRTOS or Zephyr) or bare-metal firmware, micro-ROS communicates with an off-board Linux host using the Micro XRCE-DDS (DDS for eXtremely Resource-Constrained Environments) middleware69. A dedicated micro-ROS node on the microcontroller runs hardware timer interrupts at $1\text{ kHz}$ to decode quadrature encoder signals, calculate low-pass filtered velocities, and compute motor commands1. The same node publishes state updates on topics like /furuta/state (sensor\_msgs/JointState) and subscribes to reference commands on /furuta/cmd\_vel, integrating the platform with ROS 2 nodes, trajectory generators, and Foxglove visualization pipelines57. To maintain control loop determinism, the high-frequency control loop runs within a high-priority hardware timer interrupt or dedicated RTOS task, decoupling it from the lower-priority micro-ROS serialization and transport tasks71.  
Deploying deep reinforcement learning models onto low-cost microcontrollers requires policy distillation and memory compression12. Large training architectures (e.g., Multi-Layer Perceptrons with $2 \times 256$ units) can be distilled into compact feedforward networks while preserving balancing performance12. Henrique Ferrolho demonstrated that a fully functional rotary inverted pendulum balancing controller can be compressed into a Multi-Layer Perceptron containing two hidden layers (16 and 8 neurons with ReLU activations), totaling 689 floating-point parameters1:

$$\mathbf{h}_1 = \operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{s}_t + \mathbf{b}_1) \quad (\mathbf{W}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 6})$$

$$\mathbf{h}_2 = \operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}_2 \mathbf{h}_1 + \mathbf{b}_2) \quad (\mathbf{W}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times 16})$$

$$u_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}_3 \mathbf{h}_2 + \mathbf{b}_3) \quad (\mathbf{W}_3 \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 8})$$

Once trained in simulation via SAC and fine-tuned, the network weights and biases are exported as flat constant C arrays (const float W1\[16\]\[6\] \= {...};) and compiled directly into bare-metal C++ firmware12. When deployed to an 8-bit Arduino Nano (ATmega328P running at 16 MHz without a hardware FPU), inference executes within approximately $3.2\text{ ms}$, maintaining a stable $200\text{ Hz}$ control loop1. On 32-bit platforms featuring hardware Floating Point Units—such as the ARM Cortex-M4 (STM32F4) or Cortex-M7 (Teensy 4.1)—the same inference executes in under $15\ \mu\text{s}$, leaving ample processing margin for higher-level estimation tasks1.  
For model-based optimal control (such as LQR, Linear Time-Varying Kalman Filters, or explicit MPC), firmware implementations rely on optimized linear algebra libraries1. As a header-only library, Eigen supports fixed-size matrix allocations (Eigen::Matrix\<float, 4, 1\>), which avoids dynamic memory allocation on the heap and ensures deterministic execution times31. This enables onboard execution of discrete Kalman filtering updates:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k+1} = \mathbf{A}_d \hat{\mathbf{x}}_k + \mathbf{B}_d u_k + \mathbf{L}_k (\mathbf{y}_k - \mathbf{C}_d \hat{\mathbf{x}}_k)$$

$$\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = (\mathbf{A}_d - \mathbf{B}_d \mathbf{K}_k) \mathbf{P}_k (\mathbf{A}_d - \mathbf{B}_d \mathbf{K}_k)^T + \mathbf{Q}_k$$

and full-state feedback $u = -\mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}$ at rates exceeding $10\text{ kHz}$1. For ARM Cortex-M targets, ARM’s CMSIS-NN library provides neural network kernels optimized for SIMD instructions73. Quantizing trained RL policies from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers (int8) using symmetric quantization reduces policy memory footprint by 75% and improves inference throughput on microcontrollers lacking hardware FPUs.

## **Supplementary Advanced Ecosystems: Hugging Face Robotics and Alternative Tooling Survey**

While there are no official, pre-packaged model weights or datasets specifically labeled for the physical two-degree-of-freedom **Furuta (Rotary) Inverted Pendulum** on Hugging Face—and searching "Furuta" primarily returns unrelated NLP and multimodal papers by AI researcher Hiroki Furuta—Hugging Face offers several tools, models, and libraries for reinforcement learning and robotics:

  

### 1. Pre-Trained Continuous Pendulum Models (Hugging Face Hub)

Hugging Face hosts numerous trained policy checkpoints for classic continuous underactuated pendulum benchmarks that share the same underlying continuous dynamics and trigonometric observation representations as the Furuta pendulum:

  

- **`sb3/ppo-Pendulum-v1` & `HumanCompatibleAI/ppo-Pendulum-v1`:** Pre-trained Stable-Baselines3 PPO actor-critic models configured for continuous torque balance and swing-up tasks.
    
      
    
- **`OpenDILabCommunity/Pendulum-v1-MuZero` & `Pendulum-v1-EfficientZero`:** Model-based reinforcement learning policies developed with the LightZero library, demonstrating sample-efficient continuous control.
    
      
    
- **`physicalai-bmi/efa-2-pendulum`:** Checkpoints demonstrating continuous observation-to-action mapping for physical AI benchmarks.
    
      
    

Studying the model cards and configuration files of these repositories provides exact reference hyperparameters (learning rate, entropy coefficient, clip ranges, network architecture) for underactuated inverted pendulum stabilization.

  

### 2. Hugging Face SB3 Integration (`huggingface_sb3`)

The official `huggingface_sb3` package connects Stable-Baselines3 pipelines (such as those used in Armand du Parc Locmaria's and Henrique Ferrolho's rotary pendulum repositories) directly with Hugging Face:

  

- **Automated Model Versioning:** Allows you to save, package, and push trained PPO or SAC `.zip` policies to the Hub with a single command (`package_to_hub()`).
    
      
    
- **Automated Evaluation Cards:** Automatically generates evaluation videos and logs metrics (mean episode reward, standard deviation) on the Hub repository page.
    
      
    
- **Team Collaboration:** Enables student teams to share, benchmark, and download policy checkpoints across different workstations or embedded deployment setups without manual file transfers.
    
      
    

### 3. Hugging Face LeRobot (`lerobot`)

Launched by Hugging Face, **LeRobot** is an open-source library specifically focused on end-to-end robot learning, imitation learning, and physical hardware deployment:

  

- Provides standardized PyTorch pipelines to train policies and stream actions directly to low-cost hardware actuators and microcontrollers.
    
      
    
- While widely known for robotic manipulators, its architecture supports custom environments, making it a viable modern alternative to legacy simulation stacks for deploying neural network policies onto physical motor-driven platforms.

---

Beyond MATLAB and Simscape, extending an underactuated robotics project—especially one incorporating reinforcement learning and optimal control—benefits from several specialized software ecosystems. These span multibody dynamic engines, trajectory optimization suites, modern telemetry tools, and embedded robotics frameworks.

---

### 1. Physics Engines and Multibody Simulators

Simulating the non-Euclidean configuration space ($S^1 \times S^1$) and fast dynamics of the Furuta pendulum requires numerical integrators capable of handling stiff equations and rapid velocities.

* **MuJoCo (Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact):**
* *Why it is useful:* MuJoCo has become the robotics standard for continuous control and sim-to-real workflows. Its generalized-coordinate formulation accurately handles kinematic loops and joint constraints without numerical drift.


* *Application:* You can define the Furuta pendulum via an XML (MJCF) model, calibrate motor torque constants, joint viscous damping, and rotor inertia, and achieve simulation speeds of tens of thousands of steps per second.




* **Drake (MIT Robot Locomotion Group):**
* *Why it is useful:* Drake is specifically built for nonlinear dynamics and underactuated robotics. Unlike general-purpose game engines, Drake emphasizes analytical mechanics, symbolic dynamics, and formal verification.


* *Application:* It features built-in tools for computing Regions of Attraction (ROA) via Sums-of-Squares (SOS) dynamic programming, evaluating Lyapunov stability certificates, and synthesizing time-varying LQR controllers along nonlinear trajectories.




* **Isaac Gym / Isaac Lab (NVIDIA Omniverse):**
* *Why it is useful:* Runs physics simulations entirely on GPU Tensor cores, bypassing CPU-GPU transfer bottlenecks.
* *Application:* Enables simulating thousands of pendulum instances simultaneously, reducing reinforcement learning training times for algorithms like PPO from hours to minutes while executing domain randomization sweeps in parallel.



---

### 2. Trajectory Optimization and Optimal Control Suites

While LQR stabilizes the pendulum within the linearized capture basin, generating minimum-effort swing-up trajectories can be treated as a numerical trajectory optimization problem rather than relying solely on Åström-Furuta energy shaping.

* **Crocoddyl & Pinocchio:**
* *Why it is useful:* Pinocchio is an ultra-fast rigid-body dynamics library based on spatial vector algebra; Crocoddyl builds on it to solve optimal control problems via Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) and box-constrained iterative LQR (iLQR).


* *Application:* Crocoddyl computes optimal swing-up trajectories that respect actuator voltage and torque limits, and it outputs feedback gain matrices ($K_k$) that can be tracked via Linear Time-Varying (LTV) controllers or compiled directly into embedded C++.




* **CasADi:**
* *Why it is useful:* A symbolic framework for algorithmic differentiation and numerical optimization with native interfaces to high-performance nonlinear solvers like IPOPT.
* *Application:* Useful for setting up direct collocation or direct multiple shooting to compute swing-up paths and implement real-time nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC).




* **`python-control`:**
* *Why it is useful:* A Python library replicating MATLAB Control System Toolbox commands (e.g., `ct.ss()`, `ct.lqr()`, `ct.place()`, Bode plots, Nyquist stability analysis).
* *Application:* Ideal if you want to perform rapid mathematical modeling, Riccati algebraic solving, and frequency-domain stability checks purely within Python scripts or Jupyter Notebooks.



---

### 3. Reinforcement Learning and MLOps Frameworks

A modular RL pipeline requires separation between the physics environment, the agent algorithm, and the training telemetry.

* **Stable-Baselines3 (SB3) & RL Baselines3 Zoo:**
* *Why it is useful:* The reference PyTorch implementation for model-free RL algorithms (PPO, SAC, TD3). The Zoo provides pre-configured hyperparameters, cross-validation scripts, and automatic logging.


* *Application:* Supports custom action-continuity penalties and state histories to prevent high-frequency chattering on physical actuators.




* **Weights & Biases (W&B):**
* *Why it is useful:* Real-time tracking of neural network training metrics, loss surfaces, reward convergence, and hyperparameter sweeps.
* *Application:* As used in open-source Furuta implementations (such as `Armandpl/furuta`), W&B allows tracking reward evolution across varying domain randomization bounds (e.g., varying mass, damping, or delay) to monitor sim-to-real transfer viability.




* **Optuna:**
* *Why it is useful:* A Bayesian hyperparameter optimization framework.
* *Application:* Tunes continuous reward weights ($c_1, c_2, \dots, c_6$), learning rates, buffer sizes, and entropy coefficients to optimize convergence and sample efficiency.



---

### 4. Real-Time Telemetry and Hardware-in-the-Loop Visualizers

While MATLAB App Designer provides a structured GUI dashboard, standalone high-performance telemetry visualizers can monitor high-frequency serial/UDP data streams without inducing computational latency.

* **PlotJuggler:**
* *Why it is useful:* A fast, lightweight desktop time-series visualizer specifically designed for robotics and control systems.


* *Application:* Connects directly to microcontroller serial ports (USB/UART), UDP streams, or ROS topics. It plots $\theta_0(t)$, $\theta_1(t)$, motor current, and PWM effort at rates up to $1\text{ kHz}$ with real-time zooming, FFT frequency spectrum analysis (crucial for diagnosing sensor noise), and mathematical curve transformation.




* **Foxglove Studio:**
* *Why it is useful:* A modern, modular visualization platform that supports WebSocket, serial, and MCAP log streaming.


* *Application:* Allows building custom dashboards that combine multi-signal strip charts with an interactive 3D URDF viewport displaying the physical pendulum's pose in real time.





---

### 5. Embedded Deployment and Low-Level Firmware Tooling

Bridging the gap between algorithms designed on a PC and bare-metal execution on microcontrollers requires high-performance mathematical and communication libraries.

* **Eigen (C++ Template Library):**
* *Why it is useful:* An optimized, header-only C++ matrix library.
* *Application:* Allows implementing discrete Kalman filter state estimation ($\hat{x}_{k+1} = A_d \hat{x}_k + B_d u_k + L (y_k - C \hat{x}_k)$) and state feedback ($u = -K x$) directly in embedded firmware with minimal memory overhead.


* **micro-ROS:**
* *Why it is useful:* Brings the Robot Operating System (ROS 2) directly onto 32-bit microcontrollers (STM32, ESP32, Teensy).
* *Application:* Exposes the Furuta pendulum states as native ROS 2 topics and accepts velocity/voltage setpoints over serial DDS, creating an interface to Python or C++ nodes running on an attached host PC.


* **TinyML Inference Engines (CMSIS-NN / TFLite Micro / Bare-Metal C++):**
* *Why it is useful:* Translates neural policies trained in Python into static C/C++ functions.


* *Application:* As demonstrated in embedded implementations, small policies (e.g., 2 hidden layers with 16 and 8 units) can be exported as flat C-arrays and executed in microsecond timeframes without needing a dynamic runtime environment.

## **Architectural Comparison and Synthesis**

To evaluate the software ecosystems available for the Furuta rotary inverted pendulum, the surveyed tools can be synthesized into three primary development paradigms1:

* *Paradigm A: The Classical Academic Model-Based Stack (Simulink / Stateflow / App Designer / Embedded Coder)*1. This workflow centers on the MATLAB environment. Plant models are built analytically and verified in Simscape Multibody1. Local stabilizing controllers (PID, Pole Placement, LQR) are paired with Åström-Furuta energy swing-up laws via a finite state machine implemented in Stateflow1. Hardware-in-the-Loop telemetry streams to an App Designer dashboard1. This paradigm offers rapid setup and automated verification, but remains constrained by proprietary licensing and higher runtime memory requirements on embedded targets1.  
* *Paradigm B: The Trajectory Optimization & Nonlinear MPC Stack (Pinocchio / Crocoddyl / acados / Foxglove)*9. This approach formulates control as a numerical optimization problem. Pinocchio and Crocoddyl generate dynamic swing-up trajectories and stabilizing gain matrices offline, while acados enables real-time millisecond NMPC running directly onboard9. Real-time telemetry is recorded to indexed MCAP logs and visualized in Foxglove Studio or PlotJuggler57. This stack enforces state and torque bounds systematically, though it requires greater numerical optimization expertise and careful tuning of real-time iteration solvers31.  
* *Paradigm C: The Deep Reinforcement Learning & Sim-to-Real Stack (MuJoCo / Stable-Baselines3 / Domain Randomization / TinyML)*9. Here, a single neural policy learns both swing-up and balancing behaviors end-to-end12. The agent trains inside MuJoCo or Isaac Lab using SAC or PPO, with domain randomization and latency modeling applied to bridge the reality gap10. The converged policy is distilled into a compact neural network (under 1,000 parameters) and deployed onto low-cost microcontrollers via bare-metal C++12. While this eliminates the need for manual switching logic, achieving stable real-world transfer requires careful reward shaping and accurate system identification9.

| Engineering Dimension | Paradigm A: Classical Model-Based | Paradigm B: Trajectory Optimization & NMPC | Paradigm C: Deep RL & Sim-to-Real |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Core Software Components** | MATLAB, Simulink, Stateflow, Simscape1 | Pinocchio, Crocoddyl, acados, CasADi9 | MuJoCo / Isaac Lab, SB3 / CleanRL, TinyML9 |
| **Telemetry & Visualization** | MATLAB App Designer, Simulink 3D1 | Foxglove Studio, PlotJuggler, MCAP57 | Rerun SDK, Weights & Biases, PlotJuggler9 |
| **Mathematical Formulation** | Linear state-space \+ Åström-Furuta energy1 | Direct Multiple Shooting, iLQR/DDP, RTI SQP31 | Continuous MDP, Actor-Critic (SAC/PPO)10 |
| **Embedded Footprint** | Moderate ($10\text{ KB} - 50\text{ KB}$ Flash via Coder)1 | High (embedded QP solver: $20\text{ KB} - 100\text{ KB}$)32 | Extremely Low ($<5\text{ KB}$ Flash, $<1\text{ KB}$ RAM)12 |
| **Target Microcontroller** | STM32, TI Delfino, Arduino (Coder targets)1 | 32-bit ARM Cortex-M7, Linux SBC (acados)32 | 8-bit to 32-bit MCU (ATmega328P to STM32)12 |
| **State Switching Requirement** | Requires supervisory FSM (Stateflow)1 | Smooth transition (unified OCP formulation)31 | None (unified end-to-end neural policy)12 |
| **Constraint Handling** | Saturation blocks; heuristic soft limits1 | Explicit state and actuator torque bounds31 | Soft penalties embedded within reward9 |
| **Disturbance Robustness** | Guaranteed nominal LQR margins; narrow basin1 | High (receding horizon re-planning)33 | High within randomized distribution envelope12 |

## **Technical Synthesis and Implementation Roadmap**

A phased engineering roadmap structures the implementation from initial plant modeling through hardware deployment and performance evaluation1.  
The development workflow begins with physical parameter identification and multi-body model verification1. Link geometries and mass distributions are obtained through metrology and precision balance measurements1. Decoupled unforced oscillation experiments determine joint damping ($b_1$) via logarithmic decrement calculations, while locked-rotor and no-load tests establish electrical resistance ($R_m$), back-EMF ($k_m$), and torque constants ($k_t$)5. These identified parameters populate unified URDF and MJCF model definitions, providing a consistent dynamic representation across simulation environments9. The resulting multi-body models are validated by verifying that unforced simulation trajectories match analytical ODE solutions1.  
Next, the control architecture progresses to baseline controller synthesis and simulation verification1. The nonlinear equations of motion are linearized about the upright apex to yield state-space matrices, confirming full controllability and observability1. Linear Quadratic Regulators (LQR) are synthesized using Bryson's rule to balance state deviation against control voltage limits1. An Åström-Furuta energy-shaping controller is implemented alongside the balancing law to manage swing-up from the hanging rest position1. These algorithms are integrated within a MATLAB Stateflow chart using angular capture guards and hysteresis thresholds to prevent chattering at the basin boundary1.  
Work then transitions to trajectory optimization and telemetry integration1. The baseline energy swing-up strategy is benchmarked against optimal trajectories generated via Crocoddyl or real-time NMPC using acados, evaluating trade-offs in arm excursion and current consumption9. Communication firmware is configured to stream state observations over high-speed serial UART or micro-ROS pipelines57. Connecting PlotJuggler allows immediate evaluation of encoder noise and filter delay, while Foxglove Studio provides synchronized time-series tracking and 3D URDF playback57.  
Finally, the project implements learned control via deep reinforcement learning and embedded sim-to-real transfer9. A custom Gymnasium environment wrapping the MuJoCo simulation trains an actor-critic agent (SAC or PPO) on a continuous cosine reward function with action continuity penalties9. To prepare the policy for real hardware, domain randomization is applied across physical parameters alongside transport delay buffering to model serial latency12. Once converged, the policy is distilled into a compact neural network (fewer than 1,000 parameters) and exported as static C++ arrays, allowing bare-metal deployment on microcontrollers to benchmark learned control directly against the hybrid Stateflow/LQR baseline1.
